test_public_tile_surface The modules a third-party tile author needs, and what they may import. A tile contributed from outside this package declares a CoreDefinition, speaks the row-stream ABI, names the element types its parameters take, and may render its HDL through a CoreGenerator. Those modules are therefore the authoring surface – the part that has to be reachable by someone who will never have this repository, whether that eventually means extracting them into a public distribution or publishing dau-core itself. That only stays true if the surface keeps its dependencies shallow. This guard enumerates what it may import. It is not a style rule: every name added here is a module that would have to be carried along, and a surface that quietly grows a dependency on the composition logic, the goldens, or the workload code stops being extractable without anyone noticing. The guard reads imports statically rather than importing the modules, because an import-time check would pass on a dependency that is only reached inside a function. test_registers_and_capabilities.test_handle_table_aperture_is_word_aligned_and_shares_no_address() The handle aperture the composed scan shell decodes. Its offsets are the generator’s, and they sit in free window space: above the capability block, below the lane block, overlapping nothing the base register map defines. An aperture laid over the static pipeline block would decode correctly (a shell is one personality or the other) but would leave every address in it meaning two things, which is a thing to remember rather than a property to rely on.

test_registers_and_capabilities.test_handle_table_aperture_matches_the_generator_that_emits_it() The register contract lives here, but the ADDRESSES are decoded by what dau-build emits: a disagreement is not a crash, it is a host writing a length into a generation. Pin them against the generator’s layout. Imported outright rather than skipped around: a guard that skips when the other side of the contract is missing reports the same green as one that checked, which is how this ran for exactly nobody while the aperture was being placed. The develop extra installs the dau-build this is written against, so a missing generator is a broken environment, not a reason to pass.

test_validation_at_use.test_a_copied_model_is_refused_at_the_next_boundary() -> None model_copy skips every validator, so the copy itself cannot refuse. The boundary it is handed to does: a parent revalidates its children, and check() revalidates on demand.

test_validation_at_use.test_a_frozen_model_holds_no_mutable_mapping() -> None A frozen model whose config is a plain dict is not frozen: whoever holds the model can rewrite the binding the design was priced under. There is no mutating method to refuse: the field holds a Mapping, not a dict subclass, so nothing is inherited that could write. A subclass would have been the weaker design – dict.__setitem__(m, k, v) reaches past any override – so that bypass is pinned here too.

test_validation_at_use.test_a_read_only_mapping_still_behaves_like_the_dict_it_was() -> None The freeze is invisible to everything that reads: equality against a plain dict, membership, serialization, and the hash a frozen model needs.

test_validation_at_use.test_the_canonical_form_and_the_cache_key_are_unchanged() -> None The design cache is keyed on this text. A change to how a model holds its mappings must not move it, so the pinned-hash fixture in test_composition.py keeps meaning what it meant.

test_validation_at_use.test_the_composition_boundaries_refuse_a_copied_spec() -> None Every entry point that reads a spec revalidates it first, so a spec that was copied past its validators cannot be hashed, priced or advertised.

test_validation_at_use.test_a_polymorphic_field_keeps_its_subclass() -> None CoreGenerator is a field type, so it must NOT revalidate instances: a subclass handed to CoreDefinition.generator would be validated against the base and lose its own fields. The generated cores in the registry are the proof – they load – and check() on the concrete subclass is what validates one.
test_validation_at_use.test_every_model_validates_at_use() -> None The guard: a dau-core model that is not checkable is a model whose copies nothing refuses.

test_validation_at_use.test_the_base_refuses_an_unfrozen_subclass() -> None A subclass that unfreezes itself is the quiet way back to a mutable model, so the base’s config is what a new model inherits.

test_validation_at_use.test_a_copied_generator_cannot_render() -> None A generator is a field type, so nothing revalidates it on the way in. render() is therefore its own boundary: a copied operating point must not reach HDL, because that HDL’s digest would then identify it.

test_validation_at_use.test_a_golden_refuses_a_copied_config() -> None The goldens are what hardware is compared against, so a config that construction would have refused must not produce a reference answer. The check runs once per call, outside the row loop.
test_validation_at_use.test_staging_the_hdl_refuses_a_copied_spec() -> None core_names decides which sources a build compiles. A spec copied past its validators must not make that decision.

t: Why cores are declared in config
x: The package advertises its config tree through a hydra.lernaplugins entry point (dau-core = "pkg:dau_core.config"). Anything composing Hydra configs finds the cores on the shared search path without importing dau_core. The build layer, the frontend, and the integration package all compose the same tree instead of each keeping a copy of the palette, so a version mismatch between them shows up as a composition error instead of two lists that disagree.

t: Why cores are declared in config
s: The authoring surface and the accessors are kept separate
x: A third party adding a tile needs the models, not the accessors. The authoring surface is six modules: dau_core.cores (CoreDefinition, IngestRate, StorageIntent, ParameterSpec), dau_core.design, dau_core.element_types, dau_core.generators, dau_core.models, and dau_core.stream (the row-stream ABI). dau_core.registry is not part of it, because the accessors only know about the tiles this package ships. dau_core/tests/test_public_tile_surface.py checks the separation statically by listing exactly which imports the surface may make. Each module added to that list is one more module that would have to move with the surface if it were ever published on its own.

t: Why cores are declared in config
x: A fact that would be one Python expression becomes a yaml entry plus a model field, and a typo shows up as a composition failure instead of an AttributeError where it is used. Reading the palette means reading a long yaml file instead of skimming a module. That is the price of letting more than one party edit the palette.

t: Why each tile has a golden model
x: Why each tile has a golden model Every operator tile in dau-core has a pure-Python function that computes what the tile computes. The tile’s cocotb bench runs the HDL and the function on the same inputs and asserts the outputs are identical. That function is the tile’s golden, and it defines what the tile means. No prose specification does. t: Why each tile has a golden model
s: What an executable definition makes possible
x: The bench compares against the contract. The cocotb bench does not check the HDL against hand-written expected values. It checks it against the golden over generated inputs, including adversarial ones. A hand-written expected value records what the test author believed; the golden records the contract, so the author’s assumptions do not end up in the test. The host can compute the same answer. dau-polars runs compiled scans on the golden models to get the answer the device would produce. That lets anyone check a device result without a device, and it keeps the host path consistent with the device path by definition. A disagreement has to be resolved. When a tile’s HDL and its golden disagree, the bench fails and someone has to decide which is right. These decisions are often informative. One showed that the hash-mode grouped aggregation’s golden returned partial results on overflow while the HDL returned none. The HDL was correct: the host recovers by re-running the batch, and a partial result would have been counted twice.

t: Why each tile has a golden model
s: The golden fixes more than the arithmetic
x: A golden also defines: Ordering. streaming_top_k emits rows by descending key, with ties broken by arrival, earliest first. That is part of the contract, so the tile cannot use a structure that evicts in a different order, however much faster it would be. Errors. Golden functions return a status code with their results. The code values are the tile’s status_error_code wire encoding, so the two cannot drift apart unnoticed. Domain. Keys and fields are fixed-width wires, so -1 and 0xFFFFFFFF are the same 32-bit key. Goldens wrap into that domain explicitly, because Python’s unbounded integers would describe hardware that cannot be built.

t: Why each tile has a golden model
s: What a golden does not do
x: A golden is not a fallback implementation or a performance reference. It runs on the CPU because that is where tests run; the product never executes it in place of hardware. It is written for clarity over speed, since its job is to be read alongside the HDL. It also contains no hardware structure. The golden for a systolic array is a sorted list, and the golden for a hash table is a dictionary. The tile can be built any way that produces identical output, which is what lets a tile be retimed, pipelined, or rewritten without changing what it means.

Why resource costs are measured A CoreDefinition records its resource cost as a list of measurement points. Each point is keyed by the part it was synthesized for, the clock period it was constrained to (or none, for a combinational core), and the module parameters it was built with. The registry used to allow a second form, a scalar envelope: one LUT/FF/BRAM/DSP tuple per core with no coordinates. That form was removed, and the reasons are worth recording. s: A cost only means something at a coordinate
x: “This core costs 733 LUTs” (a made-up figure) only answers the question if you also know the part, the clock, and the parameters. A scalar envelope gives the same number whichever of those you ask about. That caused two real failures. One part’s number priced another part’s build. A design targeting the Kintex was priced with a wide-predicate figure measured on the Artix. The estimate reported measured=True while mixing parts, and it hid a tile that had never met timing on the target part. Parameters that change the cost were ignored. When the shared dispatcher gained a hash decode, that mode cost 3 DSP48s where the mask decode costs none. A scalar envelope has nowhere to record that the cost depends on MODE, so a hash-dispatched design would have been priced as DSP-free and failed at implementation.

A core does not interpolate, extrapolate, or fall back to a nearby point. Ask for a coordinate it has not been measured at and it raises UnmeasuredResourceError, naming the missing coordinate. An exception is used instead of a sentinel value on purpose. A sentinel can be summed, compared, or formatted by numeric code and turn into a plausible-looking number further down. An exception has to be handled. The planner catches it and reports which measurement would fill the gap, so “this cannot be priced” is something it can tell the user instead of a wrong number. Timing follows the same rule. A point whose timing is VIOLATED is never usable as a budget: it records a failed build, not a smaller one.

Points are produced by the dau-build synthesize-cores task, one out-of-context synthesis per (part, clock, parameter) combination, and the task reports any drift from what the registry already declares. Synthesis is never run by hand, because a hand-run number loses the coordinate it was measured at. The numbers also cannot say which HDL produced them, so each entry records that as measured_from, a digest of the tile’s source and everything it imports or includes. A test recomputes the digest from the tree, so editing the HDL under a recorded envelope fails the suite until the core is measured again. Before that stamp existed, two envelopes went stale for months because one commit re-measured the coordinates it added and not the ones it changed.

s: What a measured point does not tell you
x: An out-of-context run measures the core by itself. Inside a shell the same core shares routing and placement with everything else, and its timing margin can move a long way: one tile measured +0.410 ns standalone and −0.348 ns composed, a 0.76 ns swing that turned a pass into a failure. A measurement point answers “what does this core cost on its own”, and it is an input to “will this composition close timing”. It does not answer the second question. Treat a margin under about half a nanosecond as a risk for the composed build, not as headroom. The registry notes this next to the numbers, since the numbers cannot show it.

Measuring a core means synthesizing it across its parameter space on every supported part, which takes real machine time. Until a core has been measured on a part, a design for that part cannot be priced: the estimator raises instead of borrowing another part’s number. In exchange, a Kintex build is never priced with an Artix figure.

t: How to add an operator tile
x: Put dau_<name>.sv in dau_core/hdl/ and export it from dau_core/hdl/__init__.py. Name it for what it computes. Declare a FIELD_WIDTH (or equivalent) parameter for the width and let the composition choose it. Follow the palette’s conventions: input_valid/input_ready/input_data/input_last in, output_* out, plus the status_* close-out channel. Exactly one close-out per batch; silent on success mid-chain, terminal closes out. Latch configuration on a batch’s first beat. If you hold an array in BRAM, access it from a dedicated reset-free process and keep valid bits in a separate narrow array. An array touched by an FSM process with a reset infers distributed RAM instead. Mirror the golden’s error-code values as localparams. Lint before simulating: verilator --lint-only -Wall --timing dau_core/hdl/dau_<name>.sv

t: How to add an operator tile
x: Add dau_core/tests/cocotb_benches/dau_<name>_tb.py. It drives the HDL and compares its output with the golden’s over the same inputs. It uses no hand-written expected values. Cover, at minimum: the nominal case, backpressure (a stalled beat must stay asserted and byte-stable), reset, repeated batches back to back, malformed input, and every error path. If the tile is stateful, add the randomized-delay patience harness: inject random delays on every channel and assert the emitted sequence is identical across seeds. If the tile is parameterized, run the bench at its boundaries: the declared minimum, a small value that forces collisions or short scans, and the default. Cases whose point is holding several items at once should skip at parameter values too small for them rather than being weakened to fit. Wire it into dau_core/tests/test_hdl_cocotb.py with one runner per parameter value, then: python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_hdl_cocotb.py -q -k <name>

t: How to add an operator tile
x: Append a CoreDefinition to dau_core/config/dau-core/cores.yaml; the registry is that yaml file, with no Python list beside it. Declare: name, kind: operator, module, source, a description that says what the tile does and what its contracts are, golden (as module:function), bench, count_port, contract_kind, record_words, success_close_out, and parameters mirroring your RTL elaboration guards. If the tile advertises capabilities, add opcodes, opcode_input_types, and unit_kind. A composition built only from tiles that declare none reports an empty opcode bitmap, and the planner cannot see it. Declare ingest as the rate the tile sustains: state the assumption your rate depends on and name the adversarial case rather than padding the number. If the tile owns on-chip storage, declare storage_intent. Check it loads: python -c "from dau_core.registry import core; print(core('<name>'))"

t: How to measure a resource envelope
x: The task resolves /dau-core/<name> entries through the registry, closes their dependencies, and plans one out-of-context synthesis per core. Without model.execute=true it writes the plan and stops, which is the form to put up for review or pass to someone who has the toolchain: dau-build task=tasks/build/synthesize-cores \ 'model.cores=[/dau-core/<name>]' \ model.output_root=./ooc \ model.part=<part> \ model.clock_period_ns=8.0 Under output_root you get, per core, an .ooc.xdc holding the clock constraint, an .ooc.tcl that reads the dependency-closed sources and runs synth_design -mode out_of_context, and a synthesize-cores.sh that invokes Vivado over them. The XDC is read before synthesis, so the run is constrained rather than measured afterwards. Selecting a platform instead of a bare part takes the part from configuration: dau-build task=tasks/build/synthesize-cores \ 'model.cores=[/dau-core/<name>]' \ model.output_root=./ooc \ platform=platforms/<vendor>/<board>

t: How to measure a resource envelope
x: A parameterized core costs different amounts at different parameter values, and an envelope that cannot record that will misprice a build. Pass the overrides explicitly: dau-build task=tasks/build/synthesize-cores \ 'model.cores=[/dau-core/<name>]' \ model.output_root=./ooc model.part=<part> \ '+model.parameters={<name>: {PARAM: <value>}}' \ model.execute=true An override that violates the entry’s ParameterSpec is rejected before Vivado is invoked. Run the sweep for every value the catalog can request, on every supported part, and at every clock the board can run the job at. A combinational core has no clock to constrain: give it an empty clock port ('+model.clock_ports={<name>: ""}') and the task skips both the XDC and the timing report.

t: How to measure a resource envelope
x: dau-build task=tasks/build/synthesize-cores \ 'model.cores=[/dau-core/<name>]' \ model.output_root=./ooc model.part=<part> \ model.execute=true With execute=true the task runs Vivado per core, parses utilization and timing, and reports one line per core with lut, ff, bram36, dsp, the worst negative slack, whether timing was met, and measured_from: a digest of the HDL the run read (the tile’s source, the packages it imports and the headers it includes). It also compares the numbers and the digest against whatever the registry already declares, and flags drift in either. Drift comparison requires every axis to match. A coordinate the registry has never been measured at is reported as having nothing to compare against, not as a mismatch, so an unmeasured part does not look like a regression.

t: How to measure a resource envelope
x: There is no writer: you transcribe the results. Each run becomes one entry in the core’s resources: list, keyed by the coordinate it was measured at, and the entry’s measured_from is set to the digest the task reported: # Measured via dau-build task=tasks/build/synthesize-cores. measured_from: 1:<digest from the report line> resources: - part: xc7a200tfbg484-2 clock_ns: 8.0 params: {CAPACITY: 1024} lut: 84 ff: 210 bram36: 1.0 dsp: 0 timing: met wns_ns: 3.857 Every point’s params must name exactly the parameters the entry declares, no more and no fewer, and no two points may share a (part, clock_ns, params) coordinate. A point whose timing disagrees with the sign of its wns_ns is rejected at load. measured_from is what checks the numbers after they are written. dau_core/tests/test_measured_from_matches_the_hdl.py recomputes the digest from the HDL in the tree, so an edit to the tile or to anything it imports or includes fails that test, naming the tile, until the core is measured again and re-stamped. Confirm the entry loads and resolves at the coordinate you measured: python -c "from dau_core.registry import core; print(core('<name>').resource_measurement(part='<part>', clock_ns=8.

t: How to measure a resource envelope
s: Read a thin margin as a warning
x: An out-of-context margin is measured with the core alone. Composed into a shell it shares routing and placement pressure with everything else, and the margin moves: one tile measured +0.410 ns standalone and −0.348 ns composed. Treat anything under about half a nanosecond as a risk for the composed build, not headroom, and budget a retime before composing it. A point whose timing is violated records a failed build. You can still read it, but usable_envelope() raises instead of returning it as a budget.

How to test a core This guide shows you how to check that a tile does what its registry entry says. It assumes the tile already has a golden, HDL, and an entry; see how to add an operator tile for the order those come in. Nothing here needs Vivado. The bench steps need verilator on PATH and the develop extras, which bring in the cocotb integration: pip install -e .[develop] Run the steps below in order. Each is cheaper than the next and rules out a kind of failure the next one would report in a more confusing way. 1. Prove the golden against itself The golden defines the tile, so it cannot be checked against the hardware; the hardware is checked against it. Test the golden against properties instead, in dau_core/tests/test_<name>.py: permutation invariance where order should not matter; agreement with an existing golden wherever the two overlap; boundary values, including the int32 wire identity (-1 and 0xFFFFFFFF are the same key); the algebra, if the tile has a host-side counterpart: merge(split(rows)) == one_shot(rows). python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_<name>.py -q 2. Prove the HDL equal to the golden The cocotb bench in dau_core/tests/cocotb_benches/dau_<name>_tb.py drives

The golden defines the tile, so it cannot be checked against the hardware; the hardware is checked against it. Test the golden against properties instead, in dau_core/tests/test_<name>.py: permutation invariance where order should not matter; agreement with an existing golden wherever the two overlap; boundary values, including the int32 wire identity (-1 and 0xFFFFFFFF are the same key); the algebra, if the tile has a host-side counterpart: merge(split(rows)) == one_shot(rows). python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_<name>.py -q

s: 2. Prove the HDL equal to the golden
x: The cocotb bench in dau_core/tests/cocotb_benches/dau_<name>_tb.py drives the DUT and compares its output with the golden’s, using no hand-written expected values. Build the tile’s config object once and pass the same object to both sides, so a misread config cannot cancel itself out: <!-- excerpt --> predicate = FilterPredicate(op0=PredicateOp.GT, constant0=4) kept, count = await _run_filter(dut, _VALUES, predicate, ready_pattern=(1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0)) assert kept == filter_values(_VALUES, predicate) Cover the nominal case, backpressure (a stalled beat stays asserted and byte-stable), reset, repeated batches back to back, malformed input, and every error path, asserting status_error_code against the golden’s IntEnum value instead of a literal. Wire the bench into dau_core/tests/test_hdl_cocotb.py with one runner per parameter value, then: python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_hdl_cocotb.py -q -k <name> For a parameterized tile the runner sets two coupled channels from the same pytest parameter: parameters={"SLOTS": slots} tells Verilator how to elaborate, and an environment variable tells the bench how to shape its stimulus. Set both, or the bench will exercise the default shape again

A bench that compares nothing always passes. Add your tile’s failure mode to the mutation list in dau_core/tests/test_benches_can_fail.py. Each entry edits a copy of the HDL, runs the bench, and asserts that it fails, and that it failed while running rather than at compile time. python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_benches_can_fail.py -q

ingest is part of the public interface, because a scheduler matches rates using only that declaration. Check it in the bench with the rate probe instead of trusting it: <!-- excerpt --> from .rate_probe import assert_sustained_ingest await assert_sustained_ingest(dut, "<name>", send=send, input_beats=256) It reads the declared rate from the registry, holds every sink ready, forbids gaps in input valid, and fails when the measured rate is more than one percent short, with a message suggesting either lowering the declaration or fixing the RTL. It measures input acceptance, ending at the last accepted beat, so a tile that buffers a whole batch and does its work afterwards needs a measurement that covers its drain instead.

s: 5. Prove the declared parameter space elaborates
x: The registry advertises a parameter’s bounds; the RTL enforces them in a generate-scope $error. Two guards keep those from drifting, and both are already parametrized over the palette, so a new tile is covered as soon as it is registered: python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_hdl_elaboration.py -q -k <name> python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_parameter_bounds_match_the_hdl.py -q The second one parses the $error text, so write the message in one of the recognized forms: X must be in [a, b], X must be between a and b, X must divide N and lie in [a, b], X must be a/b/c, or X must be a, b, or c. A message it cannot parse has to be added to the holdout list, and that list is itself asserted in both directions. This is the one bench tier that runs on every change. It is verilator --lint-only, with no compile and no simulation, so it takes seconds where the cocotb benches take half an hour, and it is what an RTL retype breaks. make coverage runs it and skips the compile tier; make test-hdl runs both. Because every test in that file skips when verilator is missing, a failed tool install would leave the tier green without elaborating anything. Set DAU_REQUIRE_VERILATOR=1 to turn that skip i

These walk the whole registry instead of your tile, and they catch declarations that are well formed but wrong: an entry with no envelope, a golden that does not import, a source file no entry claims. python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_cores.py -q See the registry guard reference for what each one checks. Four of them compare exact sets instead of predicates. If your tile belongs in one, a new silent-on-success stage for example, adding it to the pinned set is part of the change, so a reviewer sees it in the diff.
python -m pytest dau_core -q python -m ruff check dau_core && python -m ruff format --check dau_core

Field Type Description golden str | None The reference implementation, as module:function. Hardware results byte-compare against it. bench str | None The cocotb bench module that proves the HDL equal to the golden.

Field Type Description resources tuple[ResourceMeasurement, ...] | None Measurement points keyed by part, clock, and parameters. A combinational core’s point has no clock and answers for any. measured_from str | None Digest of the HDL closure the points were measured from (hdl_closure_digest()): the tile’s source, the packages it imports and the headers it includes. A stamp with no resources is rejected. accuracy_ulp int | None For a tile whose golden is a mathematical reference (the transcendentals): the worst deviation from the correctly rounded answer, in ULP, over an exhaustive sweep. 0 means correctly rounded. ResourceEnvelope is a count (lut, ff, bram36, dsp): a measurement point’s usable face, or the sum a composition estimate adds up to. It is not a registry shape. ResourceMeasurement has part, clock_ns, params, lut, ff, bram36, dsp, timing, wns_ns, and exposes usable_envelope(). CoreDefinition.resource_measurement(part=, clock_ns=, params=) returns the point for an exact coordinate and raises UnmeasuredResourceError when no point matches. It does not interpolate or extrapolate. The point’s usable_envelope() is what raises TimingViolationError when its timing is VIOLATED, s

Field Type Description contract_kind ContractKind | None row-stream, wide-row-stream, or the other declared framings. record_words int | None 64-bit words per input record. record_words_param str | None Module parameter that sets record_words when it is not fixed. output_record_words int | None Words per output record when it differs from the input. output_record_words_param str | None Module parameter that sets the output width. output_record_words_variable bool The output record’s width depends on configuration (for example a field mask selecting how many sum words ride each record). count_port str | None The port reporting how many records the core emitted. success_close_out bool Whether this core raises the batch’s single success close-out. Terminal tiles do; mid-chain tiles are silent on success. supports_pipeline_depth bool The core accepts generic elastic register stages without changing framing semantics. Requires a declared PIPELINE_DEPTH parameter; no build or pricing consumer reads it yet.

Field Type Description role CoreRole | None The composition job this core fills, when a composition rule turns on it. Most cores: unset. Two rules cannot be read off a tile’s ports, so the registry states them. front-unpack marks a core admissible in the optional front-stage feed transform slot, which widens packed rows into the quad rows the lanes consume. key-dispatch marks a core that routes whole records to lanes by a decode over the record’s key, and is a contract as well as a label: such a core has MODE (a DispatchMode) and NUM_PARTITIONS, and the composition enforces a power-of-two lane count for every decode but EXACT_BRANCH. A range partitioner routes by ordered splitters and declares neither.

Field Type Description ingest IngestRate | None The declared acceptance rate. Required on every operator. An IngestRate holds rows per per_cycles and takes one of three shapes. At most one scaling shape may be set. Shape Declaration Effective rate Plain rows, per_cycles rows / per_cycles Per slot scales_with_param rows / per_cycles × param Framed frames_on_param min(rows / per_cycles, param / 128) IngestRate.effective(params, declared) resolves the rate against a parameter set as an exact Fraction. The declaration is public interface: pricing and scheduling rate-match a core from it alone, without inspecting the core. It states the floor a core sustains under continuous valid input, with record and drain emission amortized over the batch. Close-out records, top-k drains and per-group records are batch-tail or per-group costs, not per-row costs. Data-dependent worst cases, such as every group key being distinct or adversarial key runs landing on one dispatcher lane, are visible in the plan and handled by the planner; they do not violate the floor. A core whose rate depends on data declares the amortized cadence and names the adversarial case in its registry comment rather than paddi

Field Type Description opcodes tuple[OperationCode, ...] Operations this core executes in hardware. opcode_input_types tuple[LogicalType, ...] Logical input types it accepts. unit_kind UnitKind | None aggregation, sort, join, membership, and so on. row_capacity int | None Bounded row capacity, for cores that hold a fixed set. A composition built only from cores that declare none of these advertises an empty opcode bitmap and is invisible to a planner matching capabilities.

Field Type Description storage_intent tuple[StorageIntent, ...] Declared on-chip or off-chip storage: role, access (owned or shared), bytes_per_unit, scale_parameter, tier_hint. load_image LoadImageKind | None The image format a two-phase LOAD accepts (bitmap-64, quad-rows). CoreDefinition.storage_bytes(params) prices the declared intents against a parameter set, validating overrides against the declared parameter specs.

Field Type Description parameters Mapping[str, ParameterSpec] Module parameters that may be overridden per instance. A ParameterSpec has a default, and optionally minimum, maximum, multiple_of, choices, power_of_two, and element_type. These mirror the RTL’s elaboration guards, and ParameterSpec.violation() is the single statement of the override rule: composition validation, the build layer, and the pricing path all call it instead of re-implementing the checks.

element_type: true marks a parameter that names what an element is, rather than how big something is. Its default and choices may then be written as type spellings, and a composition may override it the same way: FIELD_WIDTH: element_type: true default: int32 choices: [int16, int32, int64] minimum: 8 maximum: 64 The spellings are intN/uintN, float32/float64, and the fixed-point form qI.F (I integer bits including the sign, F fractional, I+F total, so q16.16 is 32 bits). They resolve to the encoding in dau_core/hdl/types.svh, which tiles include to decode a type’s width, signedness, fractional bits and float-ness. A plain signed integer encodes as its own width, so int32 and 32 are the same declaration and an entry migrated from a width names exactly the tile it always did. Bounds on such a parameter constrain the type’s width, because that is what the RTL guard they mirror checks; choices match the whole type, so int32 and q16.16 are not interchangeable despite both being 32 bits. Bus and beat widths (IN_WIDTH, OUT_WIDTH, DATA_WIDTH) count bits per handshake and are not element types. Leave element_type unset for them. A tile that includes types.svh needs its directory on the inclu

Registry-wide guards The guards are pytest tests that walk the whole registry rather than one core. They run with python -m pytest dau_core/tests; none of them needs Vivado, and only the elaboration guard needs verilator. Four of them compare an exact set rather than a predicate. Those are scoped to source_package == "dau_core.hdl" so that an installed third-party tile does not read as drift in this package’s palette. test_cores.py Registry shape, declaration completeness, and the resource-pricing contract. Guard Fails on test_every_operator_conforms_to_the_stream_tile_contract A row-stream operator whose real SystemVerilog port list drifts from the stream and status contract. Ports are parsed from the source rather than assumed. The check runs through dau_build.sv_contract.validate_stream_tile. In CI a missing dau_build fails the guard; anywhere else it skips.

Guard Fails on test_every_stamped_envelope_matches_its_hdl_closure An edit to a tile’s source, or to a package it imports or a header it includes, without re-measuring and re-stamping its measured_from. test_the_unstamped_envelopes_are_exactly_the_declared_ones A measured core without a measured_from, beyond the pinned unstamped set, which can only shrink. test_every_core_has_a_computable_hdl_closure A core whose HDL closure cannot be digested. test_a_stamp_without_a_measurement_is_refused A measured_from on an entry that records no resources.

Guard Fails on test_every_declared_parameterization_elaborates The registry advertising a parameter value the RTL’s own elaboration guard rejects. Parametrized per operator; a lint-only Verilator run over the declared parameter space, capped at 24 combinations per core.

Guard Fails on test_declared_bounds_match_the_tiles_elaboration_guard A registry minimum, maximum, or choices that disagrees with the bound stated in the tile’s own $error text. test_unparsed_guards_are_declared_and_still_exist The unparsed-guard holdout list outliving its holdouts, in either direction. test_the_python_mirror_of_the_top_k_bound_matches_the_registry dau_core.operators.TOP_K_MAX drifting from the registry’s declared K maximum. Because the bound is parsed out of the $error string, that string is machine-readable text, not a comment. The recognized forms are X must be in [a, b], X must be between a and b, X must divide N and lie in [a, b], X must be a/b/c, and X must be a, b, or c.

Guard Fails on test_every_parameter_binding_names_a_declared_parameter A .NAME() binding in a dau_* instantiation naming a parameter the target module no longer declares. test_the_identity_wrapper_forwards_every_capability_parameter The identity wrapper failing to forward a capability parameter, which would advertise it as zero.
Guard Fails on test_registry_declares_hardware_opcodes_only_for_opcode_driven_tiles A tile declaring an opcode it cannot execute, or declaring a host-computed operation as hardware.

Guard Fails on test_the_authoring_surface_stays_extractable cores, design, generators, or stream growing an import into this package’s private side. test_the_surface_declares_its_third_party_dependencies The declaration surface acquiring a runtime dependency beyond ccflow and pydantic. test_the_extraction_debt_does_not_grow The declared debt list growing, and separately, going stale. Imports are read statically rather than by importing the modules, because an import-time check passes on a dependency reached only inside a function.

Guard Fails on test_a_bench_fails_when_its_tile_is_made_wrong A bench that always passes. Each mutation edits a copy of the HDL and asserts the bench fails, and that it failed in the run rather than at compile time.

Guard Fails on test_a_generated_core_refuses_its_source_until_rendered A generated core silently resolving to a stale or absent file. test_rendering_writes_the_source_the_entry_names Rendered output landing somewhere the registry entry does not name. test_a_checked_in_core_refuses_to_be_rendered A checked-in source being overwritten by a render. test_the_operating_point_comes_from_configuration A generator’s operating point being fixed in Python rather than composed. test_each_operating_point_renders_a_different_source Two operating points collapsing to one source. test_the_rendered_source_carries_the_parameters_that_made_it An untraceable generated file. dau_core/tests/conftest.py renders the generated cores once per session in an autouse fixture, so registry-walking guards see real files.

x: Tutorial: read a tile’s contract end to end In this tutorial you will take one operator tile and follow it through every layer that defines it: its registry entry, its golden model, its measured cost, and the HDL those describe. By the end you will know where each kind of fact about a tile lives, which you need before adding or changing one. We will use streaming-top-k, the tile that keeps the K largest rows by sort key. You need dau-core installed. Nothing here needs hardware or a simulator. Step 1: look the tile up in the registry Open a Python prompt and ask the registry for it: from dau_core.registry import core tile = core("streaming-top-k") print(tile.name) print(tile.kind.value) print(tile.module) You should see: streaming-top-k operator dau_streaming_top_k The registry is a Hydra config tree loaded into the ccflow ModelRegistry, and core() reads whatever registry your application has composed. Step 2: find its meaning The tile’s golden field names the function that defines what it computes: print(tile.golden) dau_core.operators:streaming_top_k Import it and run it. Give it four rows and ask for the top two: from dau_core.operators import streaming_top_k rows = [(5, 1, 0, 0)

x: The tile’s golden field names the function that defines what it computes: print(tile.golden) dau_core.operators:streaming_top_k Import it and run it. Give it four rows and ask for the top two: from dau_core.operators import streaming_top_k rows = [(5, 1, 0, 0), (9, 2, 0, 0), (1, 3, 0, 0), (9, 4, 0, 0)] print(streaming_top_k(rows, k=2)) [(9, 2, 0, 0), (9, 4, 0, 0)] Both rows with key 9 were kept, and they came out in arrival order: the row that arrived first is first. That ordering is part of the contract. The golden’s docstring states it, and the HDL has to reproduce it exactly.

t: Tutorial: read a tile’s contract end to end
x: Ask for the resource measurement at a specific coordinate: measurement = tile.resource_measurement( part="xc7a200tfbg484-2", clock_ns=8.0, params={"K": 8} ) envelope = measurement.usable_envelope() print(envelope.lut, envelope.ff, envelope.bram36, envelope.dsp) print(measurement.timing.value, measurement.wns_ns) 1295 1196 0.0 0 met 4.35 Now ask for a coordinate that has not been measured: from dau_core.cores import UnmeasuredResourceError try: tile.resource_measurement(part="xc7a200tfbg484-2", clock_ns=8.0, params={"K": 3}) except UnmeasuredResourceError as error: print("refused:", error) You should see an error naming the missing coordinate. The registry does not interpolate between K=1 and K=5 to invent a number for K=3, because an unmeasured number that looks plausible is how a design gets priced against the wrong hardware.

t: Tutorial: read a tile’s contract end to end
s: Step 4: find the HDL those facts describe
x: The registry knows which sources the tile needs, in compile order: from dau_core.registry import sources_for for path in sources_for("streaming-top-k"): print(path.name) dau_streaming_top_k.sv This tile has no dependencies. A tile that used a shared package would list that package first; sources_for resolves the dependencies so a build does not have to. Open that file and read its header comment. It describes the same contract you saw in step 2, in the language of the hardware: a size-K systolic sorted register array where physical position encodes arrival order, which is why equal keys keep the earliest arrival without needing a counter.

It does not use hand-written expected values, so the test author’s assumptions about the tile cannot take the place of the contract. Run it if you have verilator installed: python -m pytest dau_core/tests/test_hdl_cocotb.py -q -k streaming_top_k

x: Five facts about a tile live in five places: Fact Lives in That it exists, and its shape the registry yaml What it computes the golden function What it costs measurement points on the registry entry How it computes it the SystemVerilog That the last two agree the cocotb bench Adding a tile means producing all five, in that order. dau core Hardware contracts, golden semantics, and the core registry for the DAU accelerator stack Build Status codecov License PyPI Overview dau-core holds the definitions the other DAU packages share: The core registry. Every HDL building block (streaming operator tiles, AXI stream infrastructure, shell adapters, shared packages) is described by a CoreDefinition: its module, sources, dependencies, golden model, testbench, measured resources, module parameters, and stream-contract facts. Golden models. Each operator has a pure-Python reference implementation. Hardware results are compared byte for byte against it, so the golden defines what the tile computes. Wire contracts. Register maps, stream framing structs, DMA constraints, capability advertisement, and composition specs. The package also ships the SystemVerilog for every registered core. Every operator tile has a golden, a cocotb bench under Verilator, and measured resource points. The stream infrastructure and shell adapters are tested inside the composed shells instead of one by one. Five tiles generate their source from their parameters when rendered. dau-core holds the definitions the other DAU packages share: The core registry. Every HDL building block (streaming operator tiles, AXI stream infrastructure, shell adapters, shared packages) is described by a CoreDefinition: its module, sources, dependencies, golden model, testbench, measured resources, module parameters, and stream-contract facts. Golden models. Each operator has a pure-Python reference implementation. Hardware results are compared byte for byte against it, so the golden defines what the tile computes. Wire contracts. Register maps, stream framing structs, DMA constraints, capability advertisement, and composition specs. The package also ships the SystemVerilog for every registered core. Cores are declared in a Hydra config tree, dau_core/config/dau-core/cores.yaml, with one CoreDefinition entry per core, and loaded into the ccflow ModelRegistry at /dau-core/<core-name>. The package adds the tree to the shared Hydra search path through a hydra.lernaplugins entry point, so an application that composes Hydra configs finds the cores without importing dau_core. from dau_core.registry import loaded_cores, core, sources_for cores = loaded_cores() # name -> CoreDefinition, registry order tile = core("int32-predicate-filter") # one core print(tile.kind.value) # "operator" print(tile.golden) # "dau_core.operators:filter_values" print(tile.resources) # measured LUT/FF/BRAM/DSP envelope sources_for("stream-aggregation") # dependency-closed HDL paths, in order The palette has 46 operator tiles (filters, maps, ordered and hash-mode aggregations, joins, membership, sorters, partitioners, dispatchers, temporal operators, top-k, fixed-point transcendentals, and the stateful group), 5 stream-infrastructure blocks (AXI burst reader, broadcast, record writer, write mux, row unpacker), 4 shell adapters, 3 shared SV packages, and 1 simulation model: 59 entries in all. loaded_cores() re

Each operator tile’s behavior is defined by a pure function or small model in dau_core.operators or dau_core.temporal. Tile configurations are frozen pydantic models that mirror the tile’s config ports, and the same object drives the golden, the testbench, and design emission. Their mapping fields are read-only, replace() is a model_copy that validates the result, and check() validates a model again on demand, so a copy that skipped validation is rejected before anything hashes or prices it. from dau_core.operators import ( PredicateOp, RowField, RowPredicateConfig, RowPredicateTerm, filter_rows_by_predicate, streaming_top_k, ) config = RowPredicateConfig( term0=RowPredicateTerm(field=RowField.VALUE, op=PredicateOp.GT, constant=10), ) rows = [(1, 5, 0, 0), (2, 25, 0, 0), (3, 11, 0, 0)] filter_rows_by_predicate(rows, config) # -> [(2, 25, 0, 0), (3, 11, 0, 0)] streaming_top_k(rows, k=2) # ORDER BY key DESC LIMIT 2, ties by arrival dau_core.temporal covers the time-series operators (backward as-of join, market features, time/volume/dollar/imbalance bars, rolling moments, EWMA) in an exact-integer domain: divisions are deferred to the host, so goldens and hardware agree bit-for-bit.

A shell datapath is described as data: ScanCompositionSpec names registry cores, their config-port bindings, and module-parameter overrides for a one-scan-N-lanes design. Construction validates everything against the registry (operator kinds, status-contract roles, declared parameter bounds) and raises CompositionError before any HDL is generated; estimated_resources prices a spec from the measured envelopes. from dau_core.composition import LaneSpec, ScanCompositionSpec, TileSpec, estimated_resources spec = ScanCompositionSpec( name="bar-noc-4", lanes=tuple( LaneSpec( tile=TileSpec(core="bar-aggregation", config={"cfg_mode": "2'd0"}), partition=TileSpec(core="pair-key-filter", config={"cfg_key_mask": "32'd3", "cfg_key_match": f"32'd{lane}"}), ) for lane in range(4) ), ) print(estimated_resources(spec, part="xc7a200tfbg484-2", clock_ns=8.0)) Pricing needs a part and a clock. Each core is looked up at exactly that part, clock, and parameter set, and a combination that has not been measured raises UnmeasuredResourceError naming it. Nothing is interpolated.

A quad-row operator core takes one row per beat at the rate its ingest contract declares (one row per cycle or per two cycles, depending on the tile). A wide-row-stream core takes the reader’s whole beat, SLOTS = data_width / 128 quad rows every cycle, with no dispatcher and no fan-out. The three row operators have wide counterparts (wide-row-predicate-filter, wide-row-map-alu, wide-field-sum-aggregation) that take the same configs in the same order; only the core names change. data_width must equal SLOTS * 128 or construction raises CompositionError. A wide lane cannot use the packed front unpacker, because packing saves DMA bytes at the cost of job time and a wide lane needs whole rows. from dau_core.composition import LaneSpec, ScanCompositionSpec, TileSpec, estimated_resources spec = ScanCompositionSpec( name="q6-wide", data_width=512, # SLOTS=4: four quad rows per cycle lanes=( LaneSpec( tile=TileSpec(core="wide-field-sum-aggregation", config={"cfg_field_mask": "4'b0010"}), chain=( # shipdate >= 8766 AND shipdate < 9131 TileSpec(core="wide-row-predicate-filter", config={ "cfg_field0": "2'd0", "cfg_op0": "3'd6", "cfg_constant0": "32'd8766", "cfg_combine01": "2'd1", "cfg_field1"

Multi-stage reference workflows are ccflow CallableModels with typed ResultBase results, so they can be registered and composed with Hydra like the rest of the package. dau_core.workflows.HeroWorkflow runs the temporal pipeline (as-of align, feature map, time bars, rolling moments) over the goldens and records the row count at each stage and a per-stage materialization cost (dau_core.hero). from ccflow import GenericContext from dau_core.temporal import generate_market_stream from dau_core.workflows import HeroWorkflow stream = generate_market_stream(seed=7, num_symbols=3) result = HeroWorkflow(bar_width=64, roll_window=3)(GenericContext(value=stream)) print(result.funnel) # input -> matched -> bars -> rolling row counts

dau_core.registers: the DAU magic word, register/protocol versions, register offsets, reset scopes, and the stream-job register contract (trigger/status/buffer addresses). dau_core.stream: Arrow-lite framing (BatchHeader, ColumnDescriptor, OperationDescriptor), logical types, operation codes, record-batch limits, and shared error codes. dau_core.capabilities: DMA constraints and device/operator capability models populated from a live device. dau_core.capability_contract: the composed capability advertisement a built shell publishes, derived from its composition spec. dau_core.design: the operator-unit inventory parsed back from a synthesized design’s manifest.

dau_core/hdl/ holds the SystemVerilog for every registered core, five of them generated at render time. Tiles share a 64-bit valid/ready stream and status contract: input_last ends a batch, a terminal tile closes out with a status word and count, and mid-lane stages stay silent on success. The tests run at three levels, all from pytest: text-contract checks over the packaged sources; standalone Verilator benches; cocotb-on-Verilator benches, golden-equal against the registered reference for each tile.
Requires Python 3.11 or newer. pip install dau-core Note This library was generated using copier from the Base Python Project Template repository.
